title: DBSCAN — Density-Based Clustering

blocks.t: From the notes
DBSCAN, as written
DBSCAN — Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise.
Two parameters:

items: eps ($\epsilon$) — the radius of the neighbourhood.

MinPts — the minimum number of points needed inside that
radius to call it dense.

blocks.t: Three kinds of point:

items:
Core point — has at least MinPts points within
$\epsilon$ (including itself).

Border point — not core, but lies within $\epsilon$ of
a core point.
Noise point — neither. It belongs to no cluster.

blocks.t:
Advantages: we do not need to give k, it finds
any shape of cluster, and it handles outliers — unlike
K-Means, which forces every point into some cluster.

blocks.t: The definitions, made precise

Let $N_\epsilon(p)=\{q : d(p,q)\le \epsilon\}$ be the $\epsilon$-neighbourhood
of $p$ (which contains $p$ itself).
Core point: $|N_\epsilon(p)| \ge \text{MinPts}$.

Directly density-reachable: $q$ is directly density-reachable from $p$
if $q\in N_\epsilon(p)$ and $p$ is a core point. Note the asymmetry —
this relation is not symmetric when $q$ is a border point.

Density-reachable: $q$ is density-reachable from $p$ if there is a
chain $p=p_1,p_2,\dots,p_m=q$ where each $p_{i+1}$ is directly
density-reachable from $p_i$. This is transitive but still asymmetric.

Density-connected: $p$ and $q$ are density-connected if some core point
$o$ makes both density-reachable from it. This is symmetric, and it is
the relation that defines a cluster.

A cluster is a maximal set of density-connected points. Noise
is everything in no cluster.

Operationally the algorithm is a flood fill. Pick an unvisited point. If it is
not core, tentatively mark it noise and move on. If it is core, start a new
cluster and repeatedly absorb every point within $\epsilon$ of any core point
already in the cluster — the cluster grows outward through chains of
overlapping dense neighbourhoods until it reaches a sparse boundary. Because
growth follows the data rather than a distance from a centre, the resulting
shape can be a crescent, a ring, or a spiral.

Border points are the one non-determinism. A border point may sit
within $\epsilon$ of core points from two different clusters. DBSCAN
assigns it to whichever cluster reaches it first, which depends on the order the
data is processed. Core points and noise points are always assigned identically
regardless of order. This is a known wart in the original formulation; the
"DBSCAN*" variant resolves it by treating all border points as noise.
Choosing $\epsilon$ and MinPts

Left: the k-distance plot — sort every point by the distance to its

blocks.t: The recipe
MinPts first. It is the easier one. Rules of thumb:

items:
MinPts $\ge d+1$ is a hard floor ($d$ = number of dimensions); anything
less makes almost every point core.

Larger MinPts $\to$ more points become noise, and clusters must be denser
to survive. Increase it for noisy data.

blocks.t:
Then $\epsilon$, from the k-distance plot. With $k=$ MinPts$-1$,
compute each point's distance to its $k$th nearest neighbour, sort ascending,
and plot. Points inside clusters have small $k$-distances; noise points have
large ones. The curve therefore stays flat and then bends sharply upwards —
the knee is $\epsilon$. Everything left of the knee becomes clustered,
everything right of it becomes noise.

Scaling is essential, and $\epsilon$ is in data units. A single radius
is compared against distances computed over all features, so unscaled features
break it exactly as they break KNN. Worse, $\epsilon$ has no natural default —
it must be re-chosen every time the scaling changes. Always
StandardScaler first, then read $\epsilon$ off the k-distance plot of the
scaled data.
The varying-density weakness

blocks.cap:
Three algorithms on four datasets. DBSCAN wins on circles and moons
and correctly reports "no clusters, all noise" on structureless data — but
column three exposes the flaw.

blocks.t:
One $\epsilon$ for the whole dataset. If one cluster is dense and
another is diffuse, no single radius works: an $\epsilon$ large enough to
connect the sparse cluster will merge the dense ones together, and an
$\epsilon$ small enough to separate the dense ones will label the entire sparse
cluster as noise. This is DBSCAN's fundamental limitation and it is not
fixable by tuning.

The fix is HDBSCAN (sklearn.cluster.HDBSCAN), which runs DBSCAN
over all values of $\epsilon$ simultaneously, builds a cluster hierarchy,
and extracts the clusters that persist longest across scales. It needs only
min_cluster_size, handles varying density natively, and gives soft
membership probabilities. In 2026 it is usually the better default.

OPTICS is the intermediate option: it produces a reachability plot
covering all $\epsilon$ at once, from which you can extract either a single
DBSCAN clustering or a variable-density one via xi.

High dimensions. DBSCAN is distance-based and so inherits the curse of
dimensionality from Topic 71: above roughly 10–20 features, distances
concentrate, the k-distance plot loses its knee, and the notion of "dense
region" stops being meaningful. Reduce dimension first (PCA, UMAP) or use a
domain-appropriate metric.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, OPTICS, HDBSCAN
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons, make_blobs
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score, silhouette_score

X, y_true = make_moons(n_samples=1000, noise=0.07, random_state=0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = np.vstack([X, rng.uniform([-1.5, -1.0], [2.5, 1.6], (60, 2))])  # add noise
y_true = np.r_[y_true, np.full(60, -1)]
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)          # ALWAYS scale first

# ==================================================================
# 1. CHOOSING eps FROM THE k-DISTANCE PLOT
# ==================================================================
min_samples = 8                                  # ~2*d for d=2, bumped for noise
k = min_samples - 1
dist, _ = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(Xs).kneighbors(Xs)
kdist = np.sort(dist[:, -1])                     # distance to the k-th neighbour

# Locate the knee automatically: the point furthest from the chord joining
# the first and last points of the curve.
i  = np.arange(len(kdist))
p1, p2 = np.array([0, kdist[0]]), np.array([len(kdist) - 1, kdist[-1]])
line = p2 - p1
d_perp = np.abs(np.cross(line, np.column_stack([i, kdist]) - p1)) / np.linalg.norm(line)
eps = kdist[d_perp.argmax()]
print("knee suggests eps =", round(eps, 4))

# ==================================================================
# 2. FITTING, AND READING THE OUTPUT
# ==================================================================
db = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=min_samples).fit(Xs)
labels = db.labels_                              # -1 means NOISE

n_clusters = len(set(labels)) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)
n_noise    = int((labels == -1).sum())
print(f"{n_clusters} clusters, {n_noise} noise points "
      f"({100*n_noise/len(labels):.1f}%)")

# core_sample_indices_ tells you exactly which points were CORE
core = np.zeros(len(labels), bool)
core[db.core_sample_indices_] = True
border = (~core) & (labels != -1)
print(f"core: {core.sum()}   border: {border.sum()}   noise: {n_noise}")

# Silhouette must EXCLUDE noise -- otherwise it is meaningless
m = labels != -1
print("silhouette (clustered points only):",
      round(silhouette_score(Xs[m], labels[m]), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 3. DBSCAN FROM SCRATCH -- the flood fill, ~25 lines
# ==================================================================
def dbscan(X, eps, min_samples):
    n   = len(X)
    nn  = NearestNeighbors(radius=eps).fit(X)
    nbr = nn.radius_neighbors(X, return_distance=False)
    is_core = np.array([len(v) >= min_samples for v in nbr])

    labels  = np.full(n, -1)                     # -1 = noise / unassigned
    cid     = 0
    visited = np.zeros(n, bool)

    for p in range(n):
        if visited[p] or not is_core[p]:
            continue                             # only core points seed clusters
        # --- flood fill from this core point ---------------------------
        stack = [p]
        visited[p] = True
        labels[p]  = cid
        while stack:
            q = stack.pop()
            for r in nbr[q]:
                if labels[r] == -1:              # noise or unassigned -> absorb
                    labels[r] = cid              # (border points join here)
                if not visited[r] and is_core[r]:
                    visited[r] = True            # only CORE points keep expanding
                    stack.append(r)
        cid += 1
    return labels

mine = dbscan(Xs, eps, min_samples)
print("scratch vs sklearn ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(mine, labels), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 4. THE VARYING-DENSITY PROBLEM, AND HDBSCAN
# ==================================================================
Xv, yv = make_blobs(n_samples=[500, 500, 500],
                    centers=[[0, 0], [6, 0], [12, 0]],
                    cluster_std=[0.4, 1.6, 0.4], random_state=0)
Xv = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xv)

for e in (0.15, 0.30, 0.60):
    l = DBSCAN(eps=e, min_samples=8).fit_predict(Xv)
    print(f"eps={e}: {len(set(l))-(1 if -1 in l else 0)} clusters, "
          f"{100*(l==-1).mean():5.1f}% noise, ARI={adjusted_rand_score(yv, l):.3f}")
# No single eps gets all three: small eps buries the diffuse middle cluster in
# noise, large eps merges the two tight ones.

h = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=25).fit(Xv)
print("HDBSCAN ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(yv, h.labels_), 3),
      " noise:", f"{100*(h.labels_ == -1).mean():.1f}%")
print("membership probabilities available:", h.probabilities_[:5].round(2))

# OPTICS: computes the whole reachability structure once, then you can extract
# a DBSCAN clustering at ANY eps without refitting.
op = OPTICS(min_samples=8, xi=0.05, min_cluster_size=25).fit(Xv)
print("OPTICS ARI:", round(adjusted_rand_score(yv, op.labels_), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 5. DBSCAN AS AN OUTLIER DETECTOR
# ==================================================================
# The -1 label is a perfectly good unsupervised anomaly flag.
outliers = X[labels == -1]
print("flagged", len(outliers), "anomalies")

# ==================================================================
# 6. PREDICTING FOR NEW POINTS
# ==================================================================
# DBSCAN has no predict(). The standard approximation: a new point joins the
# cluster of any CORE point within eps, else it is noise.
def dbscan_predict(db, X_train, X_new, eps):
    core_pts    = X_train[db.core_sample_indices_]
    core_labels = db.labels_[db.core_sample_indices_]
    out = np.full(len(X_new), -1)
    for i, x in enumerate(X_new):
        d = np.linalg.norm(core_pts - x, axis=1)
        if d.min() <= eps:
            out[i] = core_labels[d.argmin()]
    return out

print("new points ->", dbscan_predict(db, Xs, Xs[:5], eps))

# ==================================================================
# 7. NON-EUCLIDEAN METRICS AND PRECOMPUTED DISTANCES
# ==================================================================
db_cos = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5, metric="cosine").fit(Xs)
# metric="precomputed" accepts an n x n distance matrix -- useful for
# clustering strings, graphs, or trajectories where there are no coordinates.
Everything on one page
Summary

Idea: a cluster is a maximal set of density-connected points. Density
is defined by two numbers: $\epsilon$ (radius) and MinPts (how many neighbours
make a point "core").

Three point types: core ($\ge$MinPts within $\epsilon$), border (within
$\epsilon$ of a core but not core itself), noise (neither, label $-1$).

Algorithm: flood fill from each unvisited core point, expanding only
through core points, absorbing borders on the way.

Choosing parameters: MinPts $\approx 2d$ (floor $d+1$); then read
$\epsilon$ off the knee of the sorted k-distance plot with $k=$MinPts$-1$.
Scale features first — $\epsilon$ lives in data units.

Wins: no $k$ needed, arbitrary cluster shapes, explicit outlier
handling, robust to noise. Loses: one global $\epsilon$ cannot handle
varying density; suffers in high dimensions; border-point assignment depends on
processing order; no predict().

Cost: $O(n\log n)$ with a spatial index in low dimensions, degrading to
$O(n^2)$ in high dimensions or with a large $\epsilon$.

Use HDBSCAN when densities vary — it runs DBSCAN across all
$\epsilon$ and keeps the clusters that persist.
Interview corner
Q. How is DBSCAN different from K-Means?

K-Means partitions space into convex Voronoi cells around $k$ centroids and
forces every point into one. DBSCAN grows clusters through dense
neighbourhoods, so shapes are arbitrary, the number of clusters is discovered
rather than specified, and points in sparse regions are labelled noise instead
of being assigned.
Q. Define core, border, and noise points.

Core: at least MinPts points within $\epsilon$ (itself included). Border: not
core, but within $\epsilon$ of some core point. Noise: neither — it belongs to
no cluster and gets label $-1$.
Q. How do you choose $\epsilon$?

Plot each point's distance to its $k$th nearest neighbour ($k=$MinPts$-1$),
sorted ascending. The curve is flat for points inside clusters and rises
sharply for noise; take $\epsilon$ at the knee. Do this on scaled data.
Q. How do you choose MinPts?

At least $d+1$, commonly $2d$. Larger values demand denser clusters and produce
more noise, which is what you want on noisy data. It also sets the minimum
cluster size implicitly.
Q. What is DBSCAN's main weakness?

A single global $\epsilon$. If one cluster is dense and another diffuse, no
radius works for both. HDBSCAN solves this by considering all $\epsilon$ and
extracting the most persistent clusters.
Q. Is DBSCAN deterministic?

Almost. Core and noise assignments are order-independent. Border points
reachable from two clusters go to whichever is processed first, so their labels
can vary with row order.
Q. Can DBSCAN be used for anomaly detection?

Yes — the $-1$ label is exactly an unsupervised outlier flag, and unlike
Isolation Forest or LOF it comes free with a clustering. It works well when
anomalies are genuinely in sparse regions.
Q. Why does DBSCAN struggle in high dimensions?

Distances concentrate, so every point's $\epsilon$-neighbourhood contains either
everything or nothing, and the k-distance plot has no knee. Additionally,
spatial indexes stop pruning, so complexity degrades to $O(n^2)$. Reduce
dimension first.
Q. How would you assign a new point without refitting?

DBSCAN has no predict(). The standard approximation is to assign the new
point to the cluster of the nearest core point if it lies within $\epsilon$, and
call it noise otherwise. HDBSCAN provides approximate_predict for this.
Q. How do you evaluate a DBSCAN clustering?

Compute silhouette on the non-noise points only — including the noise label as
a "cluster" makes the score meaningless. Also report the noise fraction:
if 60% of the data is noise, $\epsilon$ is too small regardless of what the
silhouette says.

blocks.t: Step 2 – clusters. Core points within distance $\varepsilon$ of each other join one cluster. Here $P_1$ through $P_4$ form cluster 0; $P_7$ attaches to it as a border point.
Result. One cluster $\{P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4,P_7\}$ and two noise points. No cluster count was specified: the algorithm found one.

Sensitivity. Shrink $\varepsilon$ to $0.6$ and $P_7$ and some corners lose neighbours; the cluster can split or vanish. Choose $\varepsilon$ from a $k$-distance plot (distance to the $k$-th neighbour, sorted), looking for the knee.
